summary: Describes a vendor protocol from Nortel for running Multi-link PPP across more than one node, so a bundle of links can end at different devices. It specifies how the nodes discover and coordinate the bundle. This is an informational memo describing a company protocol.

eli5.summary: Normally several phone lines carry one conversation to the same house. This lets the lines end at different houses that still cooperate as one.

subtitle: Finding and coordinating PPP connections spread across multiple servers.

tldr.problem: Multi-link PPP (bundling multiple connections) breaks when different links land on different servers in a large dial-in facility.
tldr.mechanism: A discovery protocol using multicast (UDP port 581) to find where the bundle head is, and L2TP to tunnel fragments between servers.
tldr.outcome: Allows PPP bundles to span multiple servers, enabling dial-in facilities to exceed single-server connection limits.

today: RFC 2701 is an Informational specification of a Nortel Networks protocol for coordinating Multi-link PPP across multiple servers. It documents a working protocol for large dial-in facilities but is vendor-specific rather than a universal standard.

sections.title: The Multi-Server PPP Problem
sections.content:
Multi-link PPP (MP, defined in RFC 1990) lets a dial-in user open multiple connections to a single host and combine them into one logical stream. If the data load gets heavy, the user dials additional links and they are automatically added to the bundle.

But dial-in facilities at a Point Of Presence (POP) often use multiple Remote Access Servers (RASes) behind a rotary that distributes incoming calls. When the first call lands on one RAS and a second call lands on a different RAS, the bundle cannot be assembled because the second RAS does not know where the bundle head (the reassembler) is located.

This RFC specifies how RASes can discover each other and coordinate: a discovery mechanism to find where the bundle head is, and L2TP to transfer PPP fragments between RASes so they can be reassembled.
sections.eli5: When you dial in and get one RAS, then dial in again and get a different RAS, they need a way to find each other and work together to handle your multiple lines.

sections.title: Bundle Head Discovery
sections.content:
When a user negotiates Multi-link PPP on a new connection, the RAS must determine which of three cases applies: this is the first (primary) link, this is a secondary link and the bundle head is on this RAS, or this is a secondary link and the bundle head is on a different RAS.

The RAS first checks locally for the bundle. If not found, it multicasts a Query Message to the network (to multicast address 224.0.1.69 on UDP port 581) asking if anyone has the bundle head. If a Response Message is received, the RAS establishes a path to the other RAS. If no response arrives after sending queries multiple times (ROBUSTNESS times at QUERY_INTERVAL intervals), the RAS assumes it is the first link and creates the bundle head.

Query and Response messages contain a type, the endpoint identifier (which specifies the user and their machines), a random ID for tie-breaking, and a hash of the endpoint ID for fast matching. The endpoint identifier includes both the remote machine's identity and the local RAS's identity, ensuring that different rotaries do not interfere with each other.

When a RAS has the bundle head, it sends back a Response Message with a nickname (an integer) that the client can use in future messages instead of sending the full endpoint identifier. This speeds up subsequent connections.
sections.eli5: The new RAS shouts out "Does anyone have this bundle?" If someone answers, it connects to them. If not, it becomes the bundle head itself.

sections.title: Handling Contention and Configuration
sections.content:
If two RASes send Query Messages for the same bundle at the same time (which can happen if a user dials multiple links simultaneously), a contention resolution mechanism elects the bundle head. Each RAS waits until all its Query Messages are sent. Then the RAS with the lowest Random ID becomes the bundle head. If two RASes have the same Random ID, the one with the lowest IP address wins.

The winning RAS sends two Response Messages (one second apart) and indicates to its MP process that it should form the bundle head. The losing RASes stop querying and instead establish a path to the winner's RAS.

The configuration requires two mandatory and one conditional setting: Robustness (1 to 15, default 3) sets how many times to retransmit Query Messages; Query Interval (1 to 15 deciseconds, default 1) sets the interval between messages; and TTL (only for multicast, default 1) controls how far the discovery packets travel. Lower Robustness or Query Interval settings can create brief windows where multiple bundle heads might form, so operators must calibrate based on network conditions.
sections.eli5: If both RASes think they should be in charge, they flip a coin (based on random IDs). The winner runs things, and the loser connects to it.

sections.title: Moving Fragments Between RASes
sections.content:
Once the bundle head location is known, the RAS holding a secondary link must transfer PPP fragments to the RAS with the bundle head. This RFC specifies that Layer Two Tunneling Protocol (L2TP, defined in RFC 2661) is used for this purpose.

L2TP is a standard protocol for tunneling Layer 2 frames through an IP network. By using an existing protocol, the MMP specification does not need to define a new transfer mechanism, simplifying implementation.
sections.eli5: L2TP is like a tunnel through the network that carries the PPP data from one RAS to the other.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
The discovery mechanism has no built-in security. If discovery packets stay on a single physical LAN that is physically secure, software security is not needed. If packets are forwarded across a POP, security is still not a strict requirement because the scope is limited.

However, if discovery packets are allowed to cross the Internet (not recommended), RASes can be authenticated using IPSec. For increased security on a LAN or POP, IPSec may also be applied. L2TP security is handled by the protocols and mechanisms specified in RFC 2661.
sections.eli5: If the RASes are in the same secure room, they do not need extra security. If they are far apart, IPSec can protect the discovery messages.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Message type: 1 for query, 2 for response.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the endpoint ID in octets.

fields.name: Hash
fields.desc: Checksum of endpoint ID for fast matching.

fields.name: Endpoint ID (variable)
fields.desc: Variable-length endpoint identifier (remote, local, user name).
